target.title: Directors' and officers' care and diligence, including over AI

record.title: Directors' and officers' care and diligence, including over AI
record.statement: Section 180(1) provides that 'A director or other officer of a corporation must exercise their powers and discharge their duties with the degree of care and diligence that a reasonable person would exercise' in the corporation's circumstances and office. Section 180(2) treats a business judgment as meeting that standard where the director or officer makes it in good faith for a proper purpose, has no material personal interest, informs themselves to the extent they reasonably believe appropriate, and rationally believes it is in the corporation's best interests. The provision does not mention AI; it addresses how directors and officers oversee and decide, including on the adoption and control of AI.

source.instrument: Corporations Act 2001 (Cth)
source.citation: s 180(1) (care and diligence); s 180(2) (business judgment rule)

evidence.title: Corporations Act 2001 (Cth) (Official legislation register)

proposals.rationale: Research note: Text quoted from the 17 March 2025 compilation on the Federal Register of Legislation; a later compilation may exist but s 180 has not been amended in substance. Applies to corporations under the Act; not-for-profits that are companies limited by guarantee are corporations, other not-for-profits are not, so counsel decides reach. Whether a particular AI decision meets s 180 is for counsel. Research brief: data/research/BRIEF-2026-11-general-and-2026.md

target.title: Misleading conduct and false representations, including by or about AI

record.title: Misleading conduct and false representations, including by or about AI
record.statement: ACL s 18(1) provides that 'A person must not, in trade or commerce, engage in conduct that is misleading or deceptive or is likely to mislead or deceive.' Section 29(1) addresses false or misleading representations in connection with the supply of goods or services, including that goods are of 'a particular standard, quality, value, grade' (para (a)) and that goods or services have 'sponsorship, approval, performance characteristics' they do not have (para (g)); a pecuniary penalty may be imposed for a contravention of s 29(1). These provisions reach statements a business makes about its AI, and statements an AI system makes to consumers on the business's behalf.

source.instrument: Competition and Consumer Act 2010 (Cth), Schedule 2 (Australian Consumer Law)
source.citation: ACL s 18(1) (misleading or deceptive conduct); s 29(1)(a), (g) (false or misleading representations)

evidence.title: Competition and Consumer Act 2010 (Cth), Schedule 2 (Australian Consumer Law) (Official legislation register)

proposals.rationale: Research note: Operative words quoted from the 27 August 2026 compilation. The link to AI-generated statements and AI claims is an analytical mapping, not words in the Act. Financial services are covered by the parallel ASIC Act provisions (ss 12DA, 12DB), not researched here. Research brief: data/research/BRIEF-2026-11-general-and-2026.md

target.title: Ransomware payment reporting within 72 hours

record.title: Ransomware payment reporting within 72 hours
record.statement: Section 27(1) provides that a reporting business entity 'must give the designated Commonwealth body a report' within '72 hours of making the ransomware payment or becoming aware that the ransomware payment has been made'; a contravention attracts a civil penalty of 60 penalty units (s 27(5)). Under s 26 a reporting business entity is one carrying on business in Australia with an annual turnover above the threshold set by the rules, or a responsible entity for a critical infrastructure asset to which Part 2B of the SOCI Act applies. The provision reaches incidents affecting AI systems as it does any other system.

source.instrument: Cyber Security Act 2024 (Cth)
source.citation: s 26 (application: reporting business entities); s 27 (ransomware payment report within 72 hours)

target.title: Critical infrastructure risk management program covering hazards, including from AI

record.title: Critical infrastructure risk management program covering hazards, including from AI
record.statement: Section 30AC provides that the responsible entity for one or more critical infrastructure assets 'must: (a) adopt; and (b) maintain; a critical infrastructure risk management program'. Under s 30AH(1) the program's purpose is, for each asset, to 'identify each hazard where there is a material risk that the occurrence of the hazard could have a relevant impact on the asset', and so far as reasonably practicable to minimise or eliminate that risk and mitigate the impact. The annual report on the program is to be approved by the board, council or other governing body where there is one (s 30AG(2)(f)). Hazards from AI systems used in operating an asset fall within this hazard-based approach.

source.instrument: Security of Critical Infrastructure Act 2018 (Cth)
source.citation: Part 2A: s 30AC (adopt and maintain a CIRMP); s 30AH(1) (purpose of the program); s 30AG(2)(f) (annual report approved by the board)

target.title: Mandatory cyber security incident reporting for critical infrastructure

record.title: Mandatory cyber security incident reporting for critical infrastructure
record.statement: Under s 30BC the responsible entity for a critical infrastructure asset notifies a critical cyber security incident 'as soon as practicable, and in any event within 12 hours, after the entity becomes so aware' (s 30BC(1)(d)); under s 30BD other cyber security incidents with a relevant impact are notified 'as soon as practicable, and in any event within 72 hours' (s 30BD(1)(d)). Incidents affecting AI systems that support the asset are reported on the same terms.

target.title: Statutory tort for serious invasions of privacy

record.title: Statutory tort for serious invasions of privacy
record.statement: The OAIC states that a statutory tort for serious invasions of privacy, 'contained within Schedule 2 of the Privacy Act', commenced on 10 June 2025. An individual may sue where the defendant invaded their privacy by 'intruding upon the individual's seclusion' or by misusing information relating to them, they 'would have had a reasonable expectation of privacy in all the circumstances', and 'the public interest in protecting their privacy outweighs any countervailing public interest'. Unlike the APPs, it is not limited by the small business exemption. AI uses that surveil individuals or generate or expose information about them (for example deepfakes) can engage it.

source.instrument: Privacy Act 1988 (Cth), Schedule 2 (statutory tort for serious invasions of privacy), inserted by the Privacy and Other Legislation Amendment Act 2024

target.title: Privacy when deploying commercially available AI products (OAIC)

record.title: Privacy when deploying commercially available AI products (OAIC)
record.statement: Guidance for 'organisations that are deploying AI systems'. Its takeaways include that 'Privacy obligations will apply to any personal information input into an AI system', that organisations should 'update their privacy policies and notifications', that generating or inferring personal information with AI 'is a collection of personal information' under APP 3, that APP 6 limits use and disclosure to the primary purpose, and that as best practice organisations 'do not enter personal information, and particularly sensitive information, into publicly available generative AI tools'.

target.title: Privacy when developing and training generative AI models (OAIC)

record.title: Privacy when developing and training generative AI models (OAIC)
record.statement: Guidance 'intended for developers of generative artificial intelligence (AI) models or systems' subject to the Privacy Act. It states that 'Just because data is publicly available or otherwise accessible does not mean it can legally be used' to train models, that sensitive information generally needs consent, that developers 'must take reasonable steps to ensure accuracy' (APP 10), and that 'the creation of a dataset through web scraping may constitute a covert and therefore unfair means of collection' under APP 3.5.

target.title: Notice and policy for computer surveillance of employees (NSW)

record.title: Notice and policy for computer surveillance of employees (NSW)
record.statement: 'Computer surveillance' is surveillance 'by means of software or other equipment that monitors or records the information input or output, or other use, of a computer' (s 3). 'Surveillance of an employee must not commence without prior notice in writing to the employee', given 'at least 14 days before the surveillance commences' unless the employee agrees to less (s 10(1), (2)). Computer surveillance is not to be carried out unless it 'is carried out in accordance with a policy of the employer on computer surveillance of employees at work' (s 12(a)). AI tools that monitor or record staff use of computers, such as productivity analytics or copilot telemetry, can fall within these provisions.

source.instrument: Workplace Surveillance Act 2005 (NSW)

target.title: Supplying controlled technology to foreign persons, including through AI tools

record.title: Supplying controlled technology to foreign persons, including through AI tools
record.statement: Section 10A(1) makes it an offence for a person to supply 'DSGL technology to another person' who 'is a foreign person' where the supply occurs in Australia, without a permit under s 11 or an exemption ('Penalty: Imprisonment for 10 years or 2,500 penalty units, or both'). Supply includes 'the provision of access to DSGL technology'. Defence states the amendments took effect on 1 September 2024, alongside ss 10B (re-supply) and 10C (DSGL services). Placing controlled technical data into AI tools or models that foreign persons, or offshore providers, can reach may amount to supply.

target.title: Protection of personal data, including data placed in AI systems (Singapore)

record.title: Protection of personal data, including data placed in AI systems (Singapore)
record.statement: The PDPC states that 'Section 24 of the PDPA requires an organisation to make reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data in its possession or under its control in order to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks' (para 17.1). What is reasonable depends on factors including 'the nature of the personal data', the form in which it is held and 'the possible impact to the individual concerned' (para 17.2), and on the organisation's size and whether a third party holds the data for it (para 17.4). Personal data placed in AI tools or held by AI providers falls within it.

target.title: Assessing and notifying data breaches within 3 calendar days (Singapore)

record.title: Assessing and notifying data breaches within 3 calendar days (Singapore)
record.statement: Where an organisation assesses that a data breach is notifiable, it 'must notify the Commission as soon as is practicable, but in any case no later than 3 calendar days after the day the organisation makes that assessment' (s 26D(1)), and then notify affected individuals where the breach is likely to result in significant harm to them (s 26D(2)). A breach is notifiable if it is likely to result in significant harm, or is of significant scale: 'the prescribed number of affected individuals is 500' (reg 4). The PDPC guide states the assessment is to be made 'within 30 calendar days'. Breaches through AI tools or AI providers are assessed and notified on the same terms.
